title: Chorea hyperglycemia basal ganglia syndrome: A case report from Nepal
case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of involuntary, irregular, non-rhythmic, jerky movements of the left arm, gradually progressing to the left leg and perioral area. The distal limbs were more affected than proximal, and movements worsened with action and disappeared with sleep. She reported no headache, fever, seizures, weakness, or recent infections. 

Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 2 months earlier, treated with diet and metformin, but she admitted to poor adherence. She denied family neurologic disease and any use of neuroleptic, antidepressant, antihistamine, or other chorea-inducing medications.

On examination, vital signs were stable and mental status was normal. Cranial nerves and sensory testing were intact. Continuous choreiform movements were observed in the left upper and lower extremities, with decreased tone and an impersistent left hand grip. Motor and reflex testing was otherwise normal, and there was no entrainment or distraction variability.

Laboratory studies showed a random blood glucose of 412 mg/dL and HbA1c of 9.9%. Thyroid function tests, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, and vitamin B12 were within normal limits. Tests for antinuclear antibody, anti–streptolysin O antibody, and anti–NMDA receptor antibody were negative. Urinary ketones were absent. Chest radiograph and Mantoux test were unremarkable.

A noncontrast CT scan of the head revealed areas of high density in the tail of the right lenticular nucleus and right caudate nucleus, as well as hypodense regions in the right occipital lobe with encephalomalacia and multiple small lacunar infarcts in the bilateral corona radiata. MRI was not performed due to patient refusal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Stroke was considered given the basal ganglia lesions but excluded because the movements had an insidious onset and gradual progression— “Patient had insidious onset and gradual progression of symptoms.”  
2. CNS neoplasm was considered but ruled out due to absence of raised intracranial pressure signs or mass lesions on imaging— “There are no clinical features of elevated intracranial pressure or radiological findings in CT scan.”  
3. Sydenham’s chorea was entertained but excluded as there was no preceding streptococcal infection and ASO titers were normal— “There was no history of sore throat in the past. Anti-streptolysin antibodies were not elevated.”  
4. Huntington’s disease was considered but deemed unlikely because of no family history of similar illness— “There was no family history of similar illness.”  
5. Hyperthyroidism was evaluated but excluded as thyroid function tests were normal— “The thyroid function tests were normal.”  
6. Autoimmune encephalitis was considered but ruled out given preserved higher mental function and negative anti–NMDA receptor antibody— “The higher mental function was unaffected and anti-N methy D-aspartate receptor was absent.”  
7. SLE-related encephalitis was excluded based on negative ANA titers— “ANA titers were negative.”  
8. Acanthocytosis was considered but peripheral smear was normal— “The peripheral blood smear was normal.”  
9. Vitamin B12 deficiency was excluded by a normal B12 level— “The vitamin B12 level was normal.”  
10. Drug-induced chorea was ruled out since she denied use of medications known to cause chorea other than metformin— “There was no history of intake of drugs other than metformin.”  
11. Chorea in the setting of non-ketotic hyperglycemia with contralateral basal ganglia hyperdensity aligned with a metabolic syndrome— “Based on the history, laboratory findings, and radiologic findings, the diagnosis of CHBG syndrome was made.”
